nameStory: The Dwarf Ground Long-jawed Spider gets its name from a combination of traits that make it unique among its orb weaver relatives. Unlike most long-jawed orb weavers that build their webs high up in vegetation, this 'dwarf' species stays close to the ground, earning the 'ground' part of its name. The 'long-jawed' refers to the elongated chelicerae (the jaw-like parts near the mouth) that are characteristic of its entire spider family.
description: The Dwarf Ground Long-jawed Spider is a tiny orb weaver that breaks the mold of where you'd expect to find its relatives. While most long-jawed orb weavers stretch their webs between tall plants or tree branches, this diminutive spider keeps close to the earth. It's quite small, with a slender build typical of its family, and creates delicate orb webs near ground level. Despite being found across a huge range from Canada all the way to Panama, it's rarely encountered in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a small, delicate orb web very close to the ground, often just inches above soil or low vegetation, unlike other long-jawed orb weavers that prefer higher locations

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Notably small and slender even for an orb weaver, with a body that feels almost weightless if handled and legs that appear thread-thin

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Has the typical elongated, streamlined body shape of long-jawed orb weavers, with a narrow abdomen and relatively long, thin legs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web or retreats to vegetation at the web's edge when disturbed, moving with quick, jerky motions

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eyes are arranged in the typical orb weaver pattern, though they're quite small and may require close inspection with a hand lens to see clearly

habitat: Look for this rare spider in areas where low vegetation meets open ground, such as field edges, woodland clearings, or disturbed areas with sparse plant cover. It prefers spots where it can anchor its ground-level web to small plants, grass stems, or low shrubs while staying close to the earth. Given its extremely rare status in New England with only one recorded observation, it may be found in microhabitats that are easily overlooked.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin appearing as temperatures warm, likely building their first webs of the season in protected spots near the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found in their webs, mating and producing egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: May continue to be active into early fall, though this timing is uncertain given the species' rarity in our region.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as eggs or juveniles, with adults dying off after the first hard frosts.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it has been documented only once in the entire region, making any encounter with one like finding a needle in a haystack - you'd be among the first people to ever report seeing this species in our area!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with other small orb weavers, but the ground-level web location is highly unusual and should be a dead giveaway. Most other orb weavers in New England build their webs at least several feet off the ground, so finding an orb web practically touching the earth is your best clue you've found something special.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'foxi' honors someone named Fox, likely an arachnologist who contributed to spider research, though the specific person is not commonly known. This naming convention is typical in spider taxonomy where species are often named after the researchers who discovered them or contributed significantly to the field.
compareHints: Since this is the only Glenognatha species recorded in New England, compare it with other long-jawed orb weavers in the Tetragnathidae family. Unlike the common Long-jawed Orb Weavers (Tetragnatha species) that build webs over water or in tall vegetation, this species stays terrestrial with ground-level webs. It's also much smaller than most other family members and lacks the extremely elongated jaws that make other long-jawed orb weavers so distinctive.
